concept: Quick sort picks a 'pivot' element, then partitions the array so everything smaller than the pivot ends up to its left and everything larger ends up to its right. It then recursively sorts each side.
The pivot itself ends up exactly where it belongs once partitioning completes.
When the pivot splits the array roughly in half each time, that's O(n log n) — the same as merge sort, but in place, without merge sort's extra array.

The catch is that the split depends entirely on the pivot: a consistently bad pivot choice (like always picking the first element on already-sorted input) degrades performance to O(n²), which is why production implementations pick the pivot randomly or use median-of-three instead of a fixed position.
1.analogy: Sorting a deck of cards by first picking one card as a reference, then splitting the rest into a 'lower' pile and a 'higher' pile relative to it, and repeating that same splitting trick on each pile.
1.mascotDialogue: The pivot doesn't move again after partitioning — it's already home. Everything left to sort is strictly smaller on one side and strictly bigger on the other.

2.mascotDialogue: Line 9 places the pivot at its final resting index. Lines 16-17 then recurse on the strictly-smaller and strictly-larger sides — the pivot itself is never touched again.

steps.description: Unsorted input. Pivot chosen: last element (2).
Pivot 2 dropped into its final sorted index (0). Everything left is ≤ pivot, everything right is greater.

3.mascotDialogue: This pivot happened to be the smallest value, so it ends up all the way at index 0 — an unlucky pivot choice, and a good example of why pivot selection matters for performance.

4.bugDescription: The recursive call on the left side should exclude the pivot's own index (p - 1), since the pivot is already in its final position. Passing `p` instead of `p - 1` re-includes the pivot in the left recursive call, which can cause infinite recursion in some cases and, at minimum, wastes redundant comparisons re-processing an already-placed value.
4.mascotDialogue: One character off — p instead of p-1 — and the recursion loses its most important guarantee: that every recursive call works on a strictly smaller range than the one before it.

5.question: After partition() returns, what do we know for certain about the value at the returned pivot index?
5.answer: It is in its final, correct sorted position and never needs to move again
hints: This is the core partitioning guarantee quick sort relies on.
That's why the recursive calls exclude that index on both sides.
5.solution: The pivot is guaranteed to be in its final sorted position — everything to its left is smaller and everything to its right is larger, so quickSort's recursive calls correctly exclude it from both halves.
